titleStmt.title: Mode Changes in a Real-Time Architecture Description Language

analytic.title: Mode Changes in a Real-Time Architecture Description Language

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: MetaH is a language used to describe the overall configuration or architecture of a real-time avionics application. The language includes a feature called a mode, which allows the set of processes, or the connections between those processes, to be changed dynamically by the application during system operation. The language requires all possible modes of operation to be statically declared, which facilitates both automatic code assembly and real-time schedulability analysis.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: We have recently completed a prototype language and tool that allow formal specification, analysis, and code assembly for real-time embedded avionics applications. The language, called MetaH, allows a specification at an architectural level rather than at a functional or algorithmic level. The language doesn't specify what algorithms or functions individual modules compute, but instead identifies externally generated modules that are to be included in an application and how those modules are to communicate, share resources, be scheduled, are bound to hardware entities, etc. The current tool performs two functions automatically: the tool generates "glue" code that performs real-time process dispatching, communication, access synchronization for shared resources, etc. and uses this glue code t o assemble the overall application; and the tool generates and solves a timing model for the assembled system. Dynamic reconfiguration in this system consists of run-time changes between pre-specified modes of operation, which can be triggered by any software component authorized to do so in the original architecture specification. A mode change can cause a set of processes to be stopped, a set of processes to be started, and can change the pattern of message and event connections in effect. The language itself imposes a structure on the way modes (collections of processes and connections to be in effect during some interval of system operation) are defined, and consequently on the sets of processes and connections that a system will support at run-time.

The approach outlined here is distinct from a fully dynamic system in which run-time calls exist t o start and stop individual processes and in which message and event routing is performed dynamically. In exchange for a decrease in run-time flexibility, two benefits can be obtained. First, the system is heavily based on formal analysis of such factors as real-time schedulability, and a static specification of all possible modes of operation makes possible more complete and assured analyses of possible run-time behaviors. Second, automatic generation of application-specific process dispatching code and message and event communication protocol code makes possible certain improvements in space and time efficiency, and in particular facilitates the production of code having improved hard real-time performance bounds. Both of these factors, increased assurance of correctness and improved performance bounds, are important in embedded avionics systems.

Our system is similar to a number of others such as Durra [2], Maruti [8] and SARTOR [6] in its use of a high-level configuration or architec-t u r d language for composing sources. It is similar to Real-Time Euclid [lo], Maruti and SARTOR in its integration of real-time schedulability theory and analysis with code assembly. Language entities called modes and macros provide capabilities to specify hierarchical system-level state transitions, similar t o those of Statemate [5] and Durra. MetaH represents a selection, integration and extension of a variety of basic technologies in an attempt to meet the requirements of a range of avionics applications, with the objective being a transition of a number of advanced techniques and formal methods into practice. The MetaH tools have been used to develop, analyze and execute demonstrations of portions of a number of applications, including a flight management system and a missile controller. The MetaH system is part of a larger toolset designed to support the use of a multi-disciplinary, concurrent, architecture-oriented development process for the production of GN&C software [1,4].

The remainder of this paper is divided into four sections. The first section outlines the architecture specification language MetaH, with a specific emphasis on modes. The second section briefly outlines the nature of the code that is generated to glue the overall application together, and the nature of the timing model and analysis produced for the application. The third section briefly sketches how the language features can be used in two example applications, with emphasis on how modes are used. The final section discusses the current status of the system and possible directions for future work.

div.head: Syntax and Structure
div.p: At first glance, MetaH is similar to many existing structured design or object-oriented design notations [14,15]. The graphical representation of MetaH allows entities to be placed on a screen and connected together, where each entity may be defined as another collection of connected entities in a hierarchical manner, as in Figure 1. However, MetaH has a richer set of entity types and more precise semantics, precise enough to perform a rigorous real-time schedulability analysis and to automatically assemble a load image from a spec-ified collection of source files.

MetaH allows a specification of system components and connections, and attributes of those components and connections that are relevant to real-time, fault-tolerant, secure, and multiprocessor aspects of an application. MetaH provides a number of different kinds of entities beyond just processes and shared data stores. The kinds of entities in a MetaH specification can be divided into lower-level entities that describe source code components (e.g. subprograms, packages) or hardware components (e.g. memories, processors); and higher-level entities that specify how previously declared entities may be combined t o form new entities (modes, macros, systems, applications). There are rules about which kinds of entities can appear as components in other kinds of entities (e.g. a subprogram can appear as a component of a process but not a mode).

The language has both a textual and a graphical syntax defined, and tool support that will allow a MetaH specification t o be viewed and edited interchangeably in either format is nearing completion. Figure 2 illustrates the general structure of specifications in MetaH using the textual syntax. Figure 1 shows the graphic representation for the macro WIDGET interface (on the left) and the implementation WIDGET.BAR (on the right).

Entities have separate interface and implementation specifications. An interface specification (e.g. macro WIDGET in Figure 2 and on the left in Figure 1) may contain declarations of shareable monitors and packages; and/or source entities called ports and events (e.g. macro WIDGET has two ports in its interface). The language allows multiple implementations to be specified for a previously defined interface (e.g. FOO.BAR and FOO.RAB in Figure 2), where instances of these different implementations may exhibit varying behaviors at run-time. An entity implementation may contain declarations for component entities and connections between those components (e.g. P1 and P2 are components within macro implementation WIDGET.BAR in Figure 2, both of which exhibit interface FOO). div.head: Software Architectures
div.p: In this paper we will focus our attention on the semantics of three specific classes of MetaH software entities: processes, macros and modes; and on the connections between ports and events declared in the interfaces of processes, macros and modes.

A process is the most abstract source code entity in the language and is the fundamental unit of scheduling, allocation to hardware processors, and fault and security containment. A process interface may identify monitors and packages that can be shared with other processes, where shareable monitors and packages are automatically components of every implementation defined for that process interface. A process interface may identify input and output ports, which correspond to input and output buffer variables within the source code and are typed using the type system of the underlying source language. Finally, a process interface may identify output events, which are events a process will be authorized to raise at run-time using a service call. MetaH process, monitor, package and subprogram implementation specifications identify files that contain the actual source code for such entities.

Processes may be either periodic or aperiodic. While a periodic process is active (we will explain shortly what it means for a process to be active), it is automatically and repeatedly dispatched with some periodicity that is specified as an attribute of that process. An aperiodic process may have one or more events connected to it in a MetaH specification, and a run-time occurrence of that event will cause a dispatch of that process if the process is active.

Modes and macros specify collections of processes. A mode or macro interface may identify shareable monitors and packages, input and output events, and input and output ports. A mode or macro implementation may specify a collection of processes, together with connections between those processes and between the entities declared in the mode or macro interface (ports, events and shared entities in a mode or macro interface must ultimately be connected to components in an implementation of that mode or macro).

Port-to-port connections cause data to be copied at run-time from the output port buffer variable to the input port buffer variable(s) of the associated periodic processes. There is no system service that is called at run-time to send a message. Instead, each periodic process is assumed t o consume one message from each input port at each dispatch and send one message through each output port at the end of each periodic execution. Port-to-port copies are synchronized with process execution and are performed by automatically generated real-time, fault-tolerant (and planned multi-processor) communication protocol code. No message queueing is provided by the language. Where port-to-port connections exist between processes with different dispatch periods, output messages are oversampled or undersampled as appropriate. This behavior supports state update as that term is used by control engineers, where states are contained in port buffer variables of periodic processes.

Connections may also be specified between an out event and an aperiodic process (or, as we will discuss shortly, between an out event and a mode). Equivalence connections can be used to specify that shareable monitors or packages declared in multiple interfaces are, in fact, to be the same monitor or package in the final run-time image.

Not all processes in a system need be active at the same time. In particular, the language allows a specification of multiple modes of operation, where each mode may identify different sets of processes and/or different port and event connections to be in effect during that mode of operation. One or more out events from processes (or from hardware events, i.e. interrupts) may be connected to a mode. When that event occurs at run-time, a change is made from the current mode to the connected mode. When this change occurs, all active processes that are not in the new mode (including possibly the one that raised the mode change event) are made inactive. Periodic processes cease being periodically dispatched, and aperiodic processes will no longer be dispatched in response to an event connected to them. Such processes are aborted cleanly w.r.t. port-to-port communication and monitor locking. When the mode change occurs, all inactive processes that are in the new mode are made active. Process-specific initialization code is executed, after which process dispatching as described above is performed. The port and event connections in effect become those specified for the new mode.

Many applications require mode changes that affect only a subset of the processes or con-nections. The way this is done in MetaH is by allowing nested declarations of modes. A mode implementation may declare both processes and (sub)modes, where all the specified processes are active during that mode regardless of which (sub)mode is active. At run-time, a change between the (sub)modes of such a mode will activate and inactivate processes within those (sub)modes, but the processes within the containing mode re- main active. Although the scheduling of such processes will be unaffected by changes between these (sub)modes, it is possible to change connections between them by routing those connection paths through the (sub)modes.

A macro that contains a collection of processes and connections can be declared as a component of other macros and modes. The semantics are as if the macro itself were replaced by the collection of process and connection declarations. The semantics of a macro that contains other similarly restricted macros can be defined recursively. However, a mode within a macro has special semantics (which are not yet implemented). Rather than simply including that mode in the same context as the original containing macro, a crossproduct is formed between all the modes in the macro and all other (sub)modes or (sub)macros in the context containing the macro. For example, if a mode M contains two macros M. ). This enables users to specify an abstract macro, including various (sub)modes of operation, in a way that is independent of other macros. Thus, macros M.A and M.B can be developed separately, each undergoing internal (sub)mode transitions at run-time that are independent as far as the original developers of those macros are concerned.

div.head: Hardware Architectures
div.p: MetaH allows hierarchical hardware architecture specifications to be developed using memory, device, processor and channel entities. A channel is the hardware entity that supports message and event communication between processors, and ar- bitrary connection topologies may be specified.

The highest-level MetaH construct, the application, combines a software architecture with a hardware architecture. Attributes may be used to control the binding of processes to processors; monitors and packages to memories; and portto-port connections to channels. Events and certain internal system state information are (to be) communicated using a consensus protocol that provides redundancy against individual channel faults.

An important assumption of the MetaH system is that all hardware architectures provide a global periodic hardware clock interrupt to all processors that is synchronized within some given bound (i.e. all processors receive each interrupt at about the same time). This is often done using a special fault-tolerant hardware clock, though a distributed clock synchronization protocol could also be used. This allows synchronous protocols to be used for inter-processor communication.

div.head: Real-Time, Security, Fault-Tolerance
div.p: Process attributes are provided to specify the real-time scheduling characteristics of a periodic process: period, preperiod deadline, criticality, and the execution path through and individual compute times of the source modules making up a process. Additional attributes are provided to fine-tune characteristics of aperiodic processes, including attributes to adjust time-slicing characteristics (bandwidth or utilization reservation) and specify what happens when an event arrives for an executing aperiodic process. Port-toport communication is automatically performed in real-time and synchronized with the dispatching of involved periodic processes (port-to-port communication between two aperiodic processes is currently unimplemented).

The MetaH system provides three security mechanisms. First, each process executes in its own protected virtual address space. Second, time limits can be specified and enforced for process initialization and execution and for monitor semaphore locking times. Third, many run-time services can only be invoked by a process at runtime if the MetaH specification implicitly grants a capability for that operation. For example, a process can only raise an event that dispatches a specific process or switches to a specific mode if that process has been implicitly granted a capability to request that service by an event connection in the original MetaH specification.

The current implementation provides support for handling software faults (e.g. exception mechanisms), including a mechanism to notify processes that the state of a monitor may be invalid due t o an earlier fault within that monitor. Support is also provided for handling timing faults such as failure to meet a deadline (e.g. criticalities, message st at us information). Support for handling transient and permanent hardware faults is still in the design stage. The current design for t he multi-processor communication protocol (which has been hand-prototyped but is not yet automatically generated) provides tolerance to certain transient faults (lost or delayed clock interrupts, garbled messages). Work is still needed to support user control over consensus protocols (fail-stop behavior is not an adequate fault model for many avionics applications) and to integrate reliability analysis tools. Application source modules identified in the MetaH specification are assembled into processes, together with an automaticdy generated KER-NEL service call package that maps that process' source enumeration literals into an underlying global enumeration. Each application process becomes a program that is compiled and prelinked into its own protected virtual address space. The current tool accommodates simple versioning techniques ("make" facilities) so that repeated MetaH compiles do not force source recompiles unless an application source module has been changed or added (a few hundred lines of MetaH can easily specify applications having many dozens of source modules and many tens of thousands of lines of source code).

Source modules are generated that will be included in a customized kernel or executive. This code operates in privileged mode and is provided an address space that gives it access to selected application process memory locations (e.g. port buffer variables). Generated modules contain static data tables that specify attributes of the various processes, modes, and semaphores; and executable code that performs real-time communication, process dispatching, and event vectoring. This generated "glue code" actually falls somewhere between low-level application code and executive code rather than at the level of a bare-machine kernel.

Standard kernel modules do not change from application to application. These can be further subdivided into processor-independent modules and processor-dependent modules. The appropriate modules for a particular processor are identified in the MetaH hardware architecture specifications. In our prototype the processor-dependent modules provide an interface to the Tartan Ada multiple application run-time system hosted on an i80960MC uni-processor, but they could as easily interface to almost any traditional real-time operating system (e.g. real-time Mach) or bare hardware.

The design of the overall system is based on rate monotonic analysis theory. Using MetaH specifications of process period, preperiod deadline, and criticality, the code assembler derives priority, period transformation, and dispatch and time slice refill information used in the kernel's static data tables and dispatching code. Since processes may be shared by multiple modes, the final priority and scheduling data must be derived in a way that is compatible with the pattern of process sharing. Port connections and process timing information are used to generate and statically schedule assignments between processes' port buffer variables. Monitor equivalences and attributes are used to generate semaphore protocol and timing information. Finally, event connections are used to generate code that vectors events to the appropriate aperiodic processes and/or trigger the appropriate mode changes.

Much of this is mode-dependent and requires run-time selection among alternatives. For a particular mode, control code is generated that performs the communication and process dispatch-ing for that mode. The collection of all such code blocks for all modes is nested within an overall case statement, where the case selected depends on the current mode of operation. The code to vector events is similarly mode-dependent. In addition to all the modes defined in the original MetaH specification, transition modes must also be generated to activate and inactivate processes. In multi-processor systems a fault-tolerant consensus protocol must be used so that all correctly operating processors can synchronously perform the same mode change. This is greatly facilitated by the fact that the class of hardware architectures supported by MetaH all provide synchronized global periodic hardware clock interrupts to all processors, thereby supporting synchronous consensus protocols for system-wide state such as the current mode of operation.

Using information contained in the MetaH specification or produced by the code assembler, the real-time modeler generates a detailed rate monotonic model for the final application for each mode of operation. Like the kernel itself, the model contains elements common to all applications (e.g. clock interrupt handler) and elements that are application-dependent (e.g. process periods and times, monitor blocking times, interprocess communication times). The model and code are consistent with each other, i.e. the timing model is intended to be a precise model for the assembled code, with the execution time of every statement accounted for in some parameter of the timing model. Earlier experiments indicate that schedulability analysis results can accurately predict the real-time behavior of an overall system implementation, assuming the sequential compute times of individual components are known accurately [ 121.

Real-time modeling and analysis for mode changes are not as well developed, however. In our current system, mode changes may be asynchronous with respect to the periods of processes, and process initialization code is modeled as the first dispatch of that process following a mode change. There are examples, however, where mode changes may need to be synchronized with respect to the periods of specified processes and where a guarantee of more stringent real-time deadlines may be desired for process initialization. We anticipate that timing models will need to be generated and solved for transition modes as well as modes defined in the original MetaH specification [7].

Reliability analysis tools are not yet integrated into the system. The initial MetaH language design included attributes to capture fault behavior (e.g. transient and permanent fault arrival rates), together with an event expression mechanism that incorporates characteristics of both fault tree expressions and Markov processes. However, significant work remains in this area before a reliability analysis can be automatically produced from a MetaH specification.

The MetaH system (both language and runtime implementation) incorporates a number of security mechanisms. The language design includes an attribute to specify for each entity the set of security compartments or classifications that entity has access to. However, tool support is needed to capture and verity security policies. For example, an integrated modular avionics policy requires that the execution of a safetycriticality function can never be impaired by any fault in other functions [13]. Verifying this property for a MetaH specification involves performing checks on connection patterns and process capabilities, and a timing analysis based on enforced execution time limits for lower-criticality processes.

div.head: Examples
div.p: Figure 3 illustrates a portion of an avionics system in graphical MetaH. At the highest level (shown on the left), this example is similar to many actual systems in that there are two overall modes of operation, a powerup mode and an operating mode. The powerup mode implementation (not shown) would normally contain processes to perform hardware self-tests and initialize the system and then, assuming everything checks out, raise an event to switch to the operating mode. The implementation shown on the right for the operating mode is overly simplified, but shows two macros (displays and autopilot) and two (sub)modes of operation (navigation using only an inertial navigation system, and blended navigation using both an INS and a global positioning system receiver). The two navigation modes share a monitor named Kalman, which enables them to access common filter state infor-mation. The displays macro controls which navigation mode is in effect at any time by raising one of two events (shown as shaded lines emanating from the displays macro). Both the displays macro and the autopilot macro receive navigation data from both navigation modes, though since only one mode will actually be active at any time only the data from one mode will actually be transferred at any time. Each of these modes and macros would have implementations containing processes (and/or possibly (subsub)macros and (subsub)modes containing processes). These process interfaces will have ports that are connected to the input and output ports of their containing modes or macros, and will have a shareable monitor Kalman equivalenced to the Kalman monitor in their mode's interface.

Figure 4 illustrates how a redundant system might be coded in textual MetaH. Three processes execute on a four-processor system, where a processor fail-stop results in a reconfiguration to swap in the appropriate back-up process on the fourth processor. The three original processes are A, B and C in macro implementation TMR.DEM0, which are bound to Processor-1 , Processor2 and Processor3 respectively. The (sub)mode PRIMARY.PRIMARY contains no processes itself, but establishes the initial connections between the original processes (this example relies quite heavily on the use of (sub)modes to switch connections). If any process stops, one of the remaining two will raise the appropriate event t o switch to one of the back-up modes SPARE-A, SPARE-B or SPAREX, each of which contains a duplicate process bound to Processor-4. These spare modes contain both a spare process that is activated to replace the failed one and also the new connection pattern that is to take effect. If a failure is detected in a spare mode, a double fault event is raised to be handled by an outermost design (e.g. switch to a mode that shuts the system down).

One important aspect of this design is that it only works correctly if fail-stop behavior is assumed. In particular, if a defective process might erroneously raise an event then the system will erroneously transition to an incorrect redundant mode. The solution to this problem lies in the mode change consensus protocol used within the automatically configured executive itself. The use of fault-tree-like logic in MetaH event connection ..

div.head: Remarks
div.p: The current language implements both software and hardware architecture specification and timing analysis. Currently only uni-processor load images built by composing Ada source modules can be automatically produced.

However, the algorithms t o generate real-time faulttolerant multi-processor communication protocol code have been designed and documented. Although a wide variety of possible MetaH language extensions have been identified, and the integration of reliability and security analysis tools has not been performed, the current toolset is mature enough to supporting development of realtime applications and has been used to perform several real-time demonstrations.

An important but difficult-to-answer question is the degree to which the mode specification mechanism in the MetaH language provides power and convenience for specifying embedded avionics applications. We will make some comments on three types of application problems relevant to this issue.

Based on our experience to date, we feel that the mode specification ca.pabilities described above (including those features tagged as not yet implemented) are well-suited for the functional aspects of avionics applications. Mode changes used to change the set of functions currently being performed by the system seem t o be quite naturally expressed using nested (sub)modes within modes and macros. Mode transitions seem quite naturally expressed as event connections between modes (this is a form of hierarchical state transition diagram).

An area of somewhat greater concern is the specification of multiple, possibly degraded modes of operation in response to hardware failures, especially when multiple faults must be handled. Because multiple patterns of failures must be tolerated, the total number of such modes grows in proportion to the the number of fault containment regions in the hardware architecture specification, and may grow combinatorially with the number of faults t o be tolerated. Although modes as defined seem capable of handling faulttolerant systems with a moderate number of fault containment regions, additional language facilities would be beneficial.

A more general problem, and one that is not specific to MetaH modes but may be common to all architecture or configuration languages, is a need for transformational capabilities or generic configurations. The example of the redundant system in Figure 4 has an overall regular structure, and concise ways t o reuse such structures are desirable. It would be useful to be able t o specify a general structure for a redundancy scheme, then be able t o "instantiate" that structure with an arbitrary process, mode or macro in order t o make that mode or macro fault-tolerant.

A key theme in our work is the use of various formal models as a semantic basis for embedded software architectures. A single specification language is used to drive modeling and analysis tools and t o drive automatic configuration/code assembly tools. In addition to the usual benefits of a configuration language, we hope t o achieve two others. First, our language and toolset are designed to support partial specifications and partial analysis, which enables analysis and design trade-offs very early in the development process. Second, the generated models are intended to characterize the behavior of the automatically assembled applications with a high degree of accuracy, to the degree that we hope the formal analysis results will be usable during system V&V and certification. We feel that static specification of the possible modes of operation provides sufficient power for embedded avionics applications and makes it much easier to produce embedded multi-processor software whose real-time, reliability, and security behaviors can be thoroughly and formally analyzed.

div.head: Code Assembly and Analysis
div.p: Code assembly and real-time modeling and analysis are based on real-time, fault-tolerant, secure, and multi-processing technologies rather than anything resembling traditional compiler code generation. The source modules that go into the load image can be divided into three broad categories.
